Comparison on ColorMNIST, CelebA, and dSprites. Lower is better; both  SW 2 \mathrm{SW}_{2}  metrics are multiplied by  10 3 10^{3} . Entries are mean  ± \pm  sample standard deviation, — denotes an unavailable result. Boldface marks the lowest reported mean within each benchmark and metric.

Figure 1 :  ColorMNIST DR–IMMD at  n = 20,000 n=20{,}000  and  M = 2,000 M=2{,}000 . Left: two illustrative particles initialized from  P Y | A = a P_{Y\mid A=a} ; their foreground colors change during optimization while their digit identities are preserved. Right: the empirical foreground-color laws move away from the confounded observational arms and toward the oracle interventional laws. The displayed particle paths are algorithmic trajectories, not identified individual-level counterfactuals. Additional examples appear in Appendix  E.5 .

Table 2 :  End-to-end wall-clock comparison at  n = 20,000 n=20{,}000  and  M = 2,000 M=2{,}000 . Within each benchmark, all methods were run on the same hardware: an NVIDIA L40S for ColorMNIST and an NVIDIA A100-SXM4-40GB for CelebA. Each entry covers both intervention arms. Fitting and sampling times are means  ± \pm  sample standard deviations over three data seeds; totals are sums of the reported means. The final column reports total time relative to DR–IMMD.

Figure 2 :  Decoded CelebA particles during DR–IMMD optimization at  n = 20,000 n=20{,}000  and  M = 2,000 M=2{,}000 . Particles are initialized from the corresponding observational arm  P Y | A = a P_{Y\mid A=a} , and each row follows one numerical particle across optimization iterations as the empirical particle law is transported toward the interventional law  P Y ⁡ ( a ) P_{Y(a)} . Note that these are not identified individual-level counterfactual trajectories, but rather represent the distributional change needed for these particles to represent valid samples from the interventional distribution. Additional particle trajectories appear in Appendix  5 .

Table 5 :  
Ablation over the number of logged observations, before and after
particle optimization. “Initial” denotes the particle distribution
before the flow: the corresponding observational arm for the
discrete-treatment benchmarks and the logged outcome distribution for
dSprites. “Flow” denotes the DR–IMMD output. Lower is better. A dash
denotes an unreported metric; the two-dimensional experiment has neither
a separate latent-space metric nor image FID. All entries are means
 ± \pm  sample standard deviations across three data seeds. FID is
computed against the same held-out interventional reference of
 2,000 2{,}000  images at every  n n .

Table 6 :  
Ablation over the number of particles before and after IMMD-Flow.
“Initial” and “flow” denote the metrics before and after particle optimization, respectively. Lower is better. Entries are means  ± \pm  sample standard deviations across three data seeds; a dash denotes an unreported metric. Every initial entry is scored on the same  M M  samples as the corresponding flow entry, so the two are count-matched; both sliced Wasserstein and FID are biased upward at small sample size, and an initial column scored at a fixed larger count would understate the flow’s gain at small  M M .
Table 7 :  Particle-initialization ablation at  n = 20000 n=20000  and  M = 2,000 M=2{,}000 . Lower is better.
